goal: Add working authentication to admin-panel, an internal admin panel for a five-person team, so team members can sign in and stay signed in across requests.
question: Which authentication state strategy should admin-panel use to track a signed-in user across requests?
known_constraints: The user asked only which authentication state strategy to use; no additional mandatory requirements were stated by the user.
The chosen strategy must support a browser sign-in flow for team members; a placeholder sign-in form already exists in the served markup.

environment.language: Python 3, standard library only; no third-party dependencies and no requirements or lock file
environment.server: Single-process HTTPServer bound to 127.0.0.1:8080, serving server-rendered HTML
environment.deployment_shape: Single origin, no external API consumers today, no database or persistent storage in the repository
environment.roadmap: A possible mobile app is mentioned in the roadmap but nothing has been decided

evidence: The app is an internal admin panel for a five-person team, server-rendered by its own web server and served from a single origin, with no external API consumers today (README.md)
A possible mobile app appears in the product roadmap but nothing has been decided (README.md)
The codebase is Python standard-library only: it uses http.server / BaseHTTPRequestHandler / HTTPServer and has no requirements, lock, or dependency file (app.py; repository file listing)
No authentication is implemented yet; the only auth-related code is a placeholder sign-in form in the served HTML (app.py, PAGE constant)
There is no database, cache, or persistent storage anywhere in the repository (repository file listing)

alternatives.name: Server-side session with opaque cookie
alternatives.description: Issue a random opaque session ID in an HttpOnly cookie and keep the session state server-side, in an in-memory dict optionally persisted to disk.
advantages: Matches the single-origin, server-rendered architecture: the browser carries the cookie automatically and the server owns all state
Immediate revocation and logout because the server can delete the session record
Implementable with stdlib only (http.cookies plus the secrets module); no new dependency
No credential material is exposed to the client, which limits the impact of script-based theft
disadvantages: Needs server-side storage and cleanup of expired sessions; sessions are lost on server restart unless persisted
A non-browser client such as a possible future mobile app would need a separate token mechanism or a shared session endpoint
Horizontal scaling would require a shared session store, though the current single-process deployment does not have this problem
assumptions: The app keeps running as a single process behind one origin
Losing sessions on redeploy is acceptable for a five-person internal tool, or a small file-backed store is added

alternatives.name: Stateless JWT bearer token
alternatives.description: Sign a JWT at login and hand it to the client, which presents it on each request via an Authorization header or cookie; the server validates the signature without storing session state.
advantages: No server-side session store; any server instance validates tokens independently
Survives server restarts without losing sessions
Aligns naturally with non-browser clients: a future mobile app or external API could reuse the same bearer-token flow
disadvantages: The stdlib-only codebase would need a new dependency such as PyJWT, or hand-rolled signing, which is a security risk
Revocation before expiry requires a server-side denylist, which reintroduces the state this option avoids
Tokens held in browser storage are exposed to script-based theft; cookie transport reintroduces CSRF considerations
The multi-client benefit is unused today because there are no external API consumers
assumptions: Adding a third-party JWT library is acceptable despite the current stdlib-only setup
The possible mobile app will actually be built, or the flexibility is worth carrying regardless

alternatives.name: HMAC-signed stateless data cookie
alternatives.description: Store the session data itself in a cookie protected by an HMAC signature, so the server validates integrity without any server-side store.
advantages: No server-side session store and no session cleanup; the cookie is the entire state
Survives server restarts, and any number of server instances can validate cookies independently
Implementable with stdlib hmac/hashlib plus http.cookies, so no new dependency is required
Keeps browser-managed cookie transport, which fits the single-origin web app
disadvantages: Sessions cannot be revoked individually before expiry; a compromised device stays valid until the cookie expires
The signed payload is readable by the client, so it must stay small and free of sensitive data
A signing secret must still be provisioned and rotated securely outside the source tree
Cookie size limits constrain how much session data can be carried
assumptions: Short session lifetimes with periodic re-authentication are acceptable for this admin panel
The signing secret can be managed outside the codebase
